lines.text: In sixteen ninety,
envoys of the English East India Company
stood before the court of Emperor Aurangzeb,
bowed to the ground,
paid a heavy fine,
and begged for a pardon.
They had just lost a war against the Mughal Empire.
Yet less than seventy years later,
the same company would be choosing who ruled Bengal.
So how did a group of traders on their knees
end up making kings?
It began in London, full of confidence.
Francis Drake had sailed around the world,
and in fifteen eighty-eight England had beaten the Spanish Armada.
English merchants heard how rich the Portuguese had grown in the East,
and wanted a share.
So on the last day of the year sixteen hundred,
Queen Elizabeth the First gave a group of London merchants a charter,
and the sole right to trade with the East Indies.
The Dutch already held the Spice Islands,
so the English turned to India,
and its cloth.
The first steps were humbling.
Captain William Hawkins reached Emperor Jahangir's court in sixteen-oh-nine,
but the Portuguese blocked him,
and he left with nothing.
Then, in sixteen twelve, Captain Thomas Best beat a Portuguese fleet off Surat,
and an impressed Jahangir
let the English open a factory there.
In sixteen fifteen, King James sent a proper ambassador, Sir Thomas Roe.
He never got the treaty he wanted,
but he won the right to set up factories
at Agra, Ahmedabad and Broach.
On the east coast,
the Sultan of Golconda gave them a golden farman in sixteen thirty-two:
free trade in his ports for five hundred gold pagodas a year.
Then, in sixteen thirty-nine,
a Company merchant named Francis Day
got a local Nayak ruler to grant a strip of sandy coast.
There, the English built Fort Saint George.
Around it grew a town called Madras.
In the west, the luck came through a wedding.
In sixteen sixty-two, King Charles the Second married a Portuguese princess,
Catherine of Braganza,
and the islands of Bombay came as part of her dowry.
Charles had little use for them,
so in sixteen sixty-eight, he rented Bombay to the Company
for just ten pounds a year.
By sixteen eighty-seven, Bombay had replaced Surat
as the Company's western headquarters.
Bengal was the richest prize of all.
From sixteen fifty-one, the Company traded there
for a flat three thousand rupees a year,
but local officials kept demanding tolls.
In London, the Company's governor, Josiah Child,
decided to fight.
It was a disaster.
In sixteen eighty-six, fighting broke out at Hooghly,
and the English were driven out of the town.
Soon a Mughal admiral, Sidi Yaqub,
blockaded Bombay
until famine forced the English to give in.
Peace came at a price:
a fine of one hundred and fifty thousand rupees,
a public apology, and a promise to behave.
Aurangzeb forgave them, and trade resumed.
In August sixteen ninety, the Company agent Job Charnock
came back to a riverside village called Sutanuti.
When a local zamindar, Sobha Singh, rebelled in sixteen ninety-six,
the English used it as an excuse to build walls.
Two years later they bought the rights to three villages,
Sutanuti, Gobindapur and Kalikata,
for twelve hundred rupees.
By seventeen hundred, the walls had a name, Fort William,
and the town around it became Calcutta.
Charnock is often called its founder,
though in two thousand and three, the Calcutta High Court ruled
that a thriving settlement was already there before him.
Back in England, a rival company had been set up,
but it flopped, and in seventeen-oh-eight the two merged into one.
Then, in seventeen fifteen, a Company mission led by John Surman
reached the court of Emperor Farrukhsiyar.
The mission's surgeon, William Hamilton,
even treated the emperor's illness.
In seventeen seventeen, Farrukhsiyar issued farmans so generous
that the Company called them its Magna Carta:
almost no customs duties in Bengal,
its own transit passes,
more land around Calcutta,
and Bombay-minted coins valid across the empire.
Madras, Bombay and Calcutta,
three small forts on three coasts,
would become the three pillars of British India.
But first, the English had one more rival to beat:
the French.
And in seventeen fifty-seven, at Plassey,
the traders who once knelt before the Mughals
would put their own man on the throne of Bengal.
First, though, the English had to deal with the French.
In the seventeen-forties and fifties, the two companies fought three wars in the south,
the Carnatic Wars,
and after a defeat at Wandiwash, the French lost Pondicherry in seventeen sixty-one.
Meanwhile in Bengal, a young Nawab, Siraj-ud-Daulah,
was angry that the English were fortifying Calcutta without his permission.
In seventeen fifty-six, he seized the town.
Robert Clive sailed up from Madras and took it back.
Then, on the twenty-third of June, seventeen fifty-seven, the two armies met at Plassey.
But Clive had made a secret deal with the Nawab's commander, Mir Jafar.
The banker Jagat Seth Mehtab Chand and other wealthy bankers helped to fund the plot.
Mir Jafar's troops stood aside, and the battle was over in a single day.
Mir Jafar was made Nawab, and the Company collected a fortune.
The next Nawab, Mir Qasim, tried to rule on his own.
He joined the Nawab of Awadh and the Mughal emperor, Shah Alam the Second,
but in seventeen sixty-four, the Company defeated all three at Buxar.
The next year, at Allahabad, the emperor granted the Company the Diwani
of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa: the right to collect their land revenue.
The traders were now tax collectors for one of the richest regions on earth.
In seventeen seventy, famine struck Bengal.
Between seven and ten million people are thought to have died, and the Company did not reduce its taxes.
In seventeen seventy-three, Parliament stepped in, and Warren Hastings became Governor-General of Bengal.
From Calcutta, the Company now marched outward.
In the south, it fought four wars against Mysore,
until Tipu Sultan fell at Seringapatam in seventeen ninety-nine.
Governor-General Wellesley pushed Indian rulers into a subsidiary alliance:
a Company army in your state, paid for by you.
The Marathas, the last great Indian power, were broken in eighteen eighteen,
and the Sikh kingdom of Punjab fell in eighteen forty-nine.
Lord Dalhousie took over states whose rulers died without a natural heir:
the Doctrine of Lapse.
He also brought railways: India's first passenger train ran from Bombay to Thane in eighteen fifty-three.
But anger had been building: over lost kingdoms, heavy taxes, and new rifle cartridges
rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat.
On the tenth of May, eighteen fifty-seven, soldiers at Meerut rose up and marched to Delhi.
They proclaimed the old emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, their leader.
The revolt spread across the north: to Kanpur, Lucknow and Jhansi,
where Rani Lakshmibai, who had lost her kingdom to the Doctrine of Lapse, became one of its leaders.
It took the British more than a year to crush the revolt, and both sides committed atrocities against civilians.
Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled to Rangoon, and the Mughal dynasty came to an end.
In eighteen fifty-eight, Parliament took India away from the East India Company.
India was now ruled directly by the British Crown.
That November, the British offered a pardon to all rebels not involved in murder.
The old company itself was finally dissolved in eighteen seventy-four.
In eighteen seventy-seven, Victoria was declared Empress of India.
Railways and ports spread, but thinkers like Dadabhai Naoroji argued that India's wealth was being drained to Britain.
In eighteen eighty-five, educated Indians founded the Indian National Congress in Bombay.
At first, it asked for reforms with petitions and resolutions.
Then, in nineteen-oh-five, Viceroy Curzon split Bengal in two,
and Bengal rose in protest.
People boycotted British goods and bought Indian-made ones: Swadeshi.
In nineteen eleven, the partition was reversed, and the capital moved from Calcutta to Delhi.
In nineteen fifteen, Mohandas Gandhi came home from South Africa.
In April nineteen nineteen, at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar,
British troops fired on an unarmed crowd, and hundreds were killed.
In nineteen twenty, Gandhi answered with non-violent non-cooperation:
Indians gave up foreign cloth, returned British titles and resigned from their posts.
In nineteen thirty, he walked about two hundred and forty miles to the sea at Dandi, to make salt and break the salt law.
Newspapers around the world reported it.
In nineteen forty-two, during the Second World War, Congress told the British: Quit India.
Almost all its leaders were jailed, while Subhas Chandra Bose led the Indian National Army against the British from South-East Asia.
In July nineteen forty-seven, the British Parliament passed the Indian Independence Act.
British India was divided into two countries, India and Pakistan.
At midnight on the fifteenth of August, nineteen forty-seven, India became free.
Partition drove between twelve and twenty million people from their homes.
Three hundred and forty-seven years after a queen signed a charter for London merchants,
the story that began with traders on their knees
ended with a free India choosing its own way.
